title: The clear gem
hookLine: the jhana similes, and a clear gem with a thread seen through it

lines: A GLASS BEAD HELD TO THE LIGHT.
THE THREAD INSIDE, PLAIN TO SEE.
cards: Hold a clear marble or a glass bead up to the light, and you can see right through it. If a thread runs through the middle, you see the thread too, its color, how it bends. Nothing is hidden.

The second long discourse ends its account of meditation with an object like that: a gem, cut and polished, so clear that the thread strung through it is plain to see. But first, four pictures of a mind settling.

teach.b: The monk has set down the five hindrances, and joy arises. Then come the four absorptions, the jhanas, each with a picture.
In the first, joy and ease soak through the whole body, like a bath attendant kneading soap powder with water until the ball of powder is moist all through, and nothing drips.
In the second, like a deep lake fed by a spring from underneath, no stream flowing in, no rain: cool water wells up from within and fills it.
In the third, like lotuses growing underwater, never breaking the surface, soaked from root to tip.

teach.h: LOTUSES UNDER WATER, A WHITE CLOTH
teach.b: In the fourth, like someone sitting wrapped head to foot in a clean white cloth, no part of the body uncovered. Then the mind is concentrated, purified, bright, workable, steady, and the monk turns it toward knowing.

This body is made of the four elements, born of mother and father, kept going by rice and porridge, bound to wear away and break apart. And this consciousness of mine rests on it and is tied to it. Here's the gem.

teach.h: THE GEM, AND THE THREAD THROUGH IT
teach.b: A beautiful veluriya, a beryl, eight-faceted, well cut, clear and flawless, and through it runs a thread: blue, yellow, red, white or brown.
Someone with good eyes takes it in hand and sees: this is the gem, and this is the thread running through it. That's the image of insight here. Not a vision of something far away.
Just seeing, clearly, what's already in your hand: a body, and the awareness strung through it.

how: Meditation teachers in several Buddhist traditions use the four jhana similes from this discourse to describe deepening concentration, and then guide practitioners to turn the settled mind toward seeing body and mind clearly.

o: a lotus that grows under the water
a clean white cloth for meditation
a beryl, a clear and flawless gem

games.q: the clear gem: tap the pairs.
p: a lake fed by a spring below
wrapped head to foot in white cloth

s: the gem image shows a vision of something far away
it's seeing clearly what's already in your hand: the body and the consciousness running through it.
in the first simile, the soaked ball of soap powder doesn't drip
joy and ease fill the whole body without spilling over.
the second jhana's lake is filled by rain and streams
no stream, no rain: cool water wells up from a spring underneath.

games.q: the monk's mind is concentrated, bright and steady after the fourth jhana. what does DN 2 say he turns it toward first?
o: knowing the body and the consciousness bound to it.
games.why: he sees the body made of the four elements, and consciousness tied to it, like a thread seen through a clear gem.

practice: Feel the body as one whole shape, sitting here, weight, warmth, breath: that's the gem. Now notice the knowing of it, the thread, without trying to separate the two; when you drift, come back to the shape, and the knowing.

wordCard.voice: Veluriya. A beryl, flawless and clear: a settled mind sees the body and the consciousness running through it, as plainly as a thread through this gem.

orig.note: Pali veluriya: a precious stone, often translated beryl (some say lapis or cat's eye). the gem with the thread in DN 2.

carryVoice: Your line: the gem and the thread. Nothing hidden, nothing far away. Day five hundred thirty.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta, the jhana similes and the beryl simile
